extracted.intended_audience: employers, human resources managers, payroll administrators, labor and employment attorneys, and employees assessing FLSA exemption status
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply Department of Labor criteria for determining whether employees qualify as exempt under FLSA categories (administrative, professional, computer, outside sales, and salary-level requirements). Includes duties tests, examples, exclusions, and territory salary variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative exemption — duties directly related to management or general business operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties that are 'directly and closely related to the employee's exempt functions' (management or general business operations) may meet the administrative exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that helps operate the business and involves significant matters of business operations can be administrative-exempt work. The rule distinguishes routine tasks from those closely related to management functions; context and relation to exempt functions are determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative exemption — human resources managers vs personnel clerks
rubrics_metrics.description: Human resources managers who formulate, interpret, or implement employment policies and management consultants who propose organizational changes generally meet duties requirements for the administrative exemption; personnel clerks who merely 'screen' applicants for minimum qualifications generally do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If interviewing/screening functions are performed by the HR/personnel manager who makes hiring decisions or recommends hires, that work—even if routine—can be exempt because it is directly and closely related to exempt functions. Conversely, clerks who only collect minimum-qualification data and reject unqualified applicants typically are nonexempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative exemption — purchasing agents with binding authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchasing agents who have authority to bind the company on significant purchases generally meet administrative-exemption duties requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such agents qualify even if they must consult top management for purchases exceeding certain limits; authority to commit the employer on significant purchases is the key factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative exemption — ordinary inspection work excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary inspection work generally does not meet duties requirements for the administrative exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspectors performing specialized work along standardized lines using well-established techniques/procedures catalogued in manuals, relying on skills from training or experience, with only limited leeway, are typically nonexempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative exemption — examiners/graders excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees usually called examiners or graders (e.g., lumber graders) generally do not meet duties requirements for the administrative exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that consists of comparing products to established written standards—where the employee's memory may substitute for a manual—remains nonexempt; mere substitution of memory for the manual does not convert the work to exempt work requiring discretion and independent judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative exemption — comparison shopping vs buyer evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee who merely reports competitor prices does not qualify for the administrative exemption; a buyer who evaluates competitor-price reports to set the employer's prices generally meets the duties requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critical distinction is whether the employee exercises evaluative judgment and ties reports to business decisions (exempt) versus merely collecting factual information (nonexempt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative exemption — public sector inspectors/investigators excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Public sector inspectors or investigators (fire prevention/safety, building/construction, health/sanitation, environmental/soils specialists, etc.) generally do not meet duties requirements for the administrative exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their work typically is not directly related to management or general business operations and instead involves use of technical skills to gather factual information, apply standards or procedures, and determine compliance—characteristics of nonexempt work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational establishments — administrative-capacity inclusion (salary and primary duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees 'employed in a bona fide administrative capacity' in educational establishments include employees who (1) are compensated on a salary or fee basis at not less than §541.600 (or on a salary basis at least equal to the entrance salary for teachers at that establishment) and (2) whose primary duty is performing administrative functions directly related to academic instruction or training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the compensation requirement and the academic-administration primary-duty requirement must be satisfied for this inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'educational establishment'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term means an elementary or secondary school system, an institution of higher education, or other educational institution; includes special schools for disabled or gifted children and both public/private and for-profit/nonprofit schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For post‑secondary career programs, relevant factors include state licensing or accreditation by a nationally recognized accrediting organization; classification under State law determines elementary/secondary status; no distinction is drawn between public/private or profit status for the exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic-administration primary duty — scope and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Performing administrative functions directly related to academic instruction or training’ means work related to academic operations and functions in a school rather than general business administration; jobs outside the educational field are not academic administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of academic administrative functions: superintendent, school system heads and assistants (curriculum, testing, grading standards), principals and vice-principals, higher-education department heads, academic counselors (testing, advising). Excluded: building management/maintenance, student health roles, social workers, psychologists, lunch room managers, dietitians (these may qualify under other exemption sections if requirements are met).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional exemption — general rule (salary/primary duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a bona fide professional under section 13(a)(1), an employee must (1) be compensated on a salary or fee basis at not less than §541.600 and (2) have a primary duty consisting of either (i) work requiring knowledge of an advanced type in a field of science or learning customarily acquired by prolonged specialized instruction, or (ii) work requiring invention, imagination, originality or talent in a recognized field of artistic or creative endeavor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology cross‑references: salary basis (§541.602), fee basis (§541.605), board/lodging (§541.606), and primary duty (§541.700).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learned professional exemption — three-element primary-duty test
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary duty must: (1) be work requiring advanced knowledge; (2) the advanced knowledge must be in a field of science or learning; and (3) the advanced knowledge must be customarily acquired by a prolonged course of specialized intellectual instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three elements must be met to qualify as a learned professional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work requiring advanced knowledge — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Means work predominantly intellectual in character and requiring consistent exercise of discretion and judgment, distinguished from routine mental, manual, mechanical or physical work; generally involves analyzing, interpreting, or making deductions from varying facts or circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advanced knowledge cannot be attained at the high school level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of science or learning — scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes traditional professions: law, medicine, theology, accounting, actuarial computation, engineering, architecture, teaching, physical/chemical/biological sciences, pharmacy, and similar occupations with recognized professional status, as distinct from mechanical arts or skilled trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occupation must be recognized as a profession, not merely skilled trade even if advanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customarily acquired by prolonged specialized instruction — evidence and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Restricts exemption to professions where specialized academic training is a standard prerequisite for entry; prima facie evidence is possession of the appropriate academic degree, but equivalent combination of work experience and instruction may suffice in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemption is not available for occupations usually performed with general academic degrees, apprenticeship training, or routine process training, nor for occupations where most employees gained skill primarily through experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of learned professionals (occupational guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists occupations that generally meet or do not meet learned-professional duties requirements: (e.g., registered/certified medical technologists, registered nurses, dental hygienists, physician assistants, certified public accountants, chefs with four‑year specialized degrees) and notes paralegals and certain health workers generally do not qualify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each example includes the conditions under which the occupation meets or fails to meet the exemption (e.g., degree/certification requirements, routine nature of work). Paralegals may qualify only if they possess advanced specialized degrees in other professional fields and apply that advanced knowledge in their duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of learned-professional categories over time
rubrics_metrics.description: As academic training broadens and specialized degrees emerge, new occupations may acquire learned-profession characteristics if an advanced specialized degree becomes a standard requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accrediting and certifying organizations that create standardized curriculums and certifications may indicate that an occupation has acquired learned-profession characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative professional exemption — primary duty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify, primary duty must be performing work requiring invention, imagination, originality or talent in a recognized artistic or creative field, as opposed to routine mental/manual/mechanical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that can be produced by a person with general ability/training is not covered; the degree of invention/originality is assessed case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized creative fields and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognized fields include music, writing, acting, graphic arts; occupations generally meeting the requirement include actors, musicians, composers, soloists, painters given only subject matter, certain cartoonists, essayists/novelists/screen‑play writers (typically self-employed), and responsible advertising writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, copyists, animators of motion‑picture cartoons, or photo retouchers generally do not meet the creative-professional exemption because their work is not sufficiently creative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists — creative professional application
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists may qualify if their primary duty requires invention, imagination, originality or talent (e.g., investigative interviews, analysis/interpretation, editorials, opinion columns, on‑air performance); journalists whose work consists of collecting/organizing routine or public information, rewriting press releases, or work subject to substantial employer control do not qualify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualification depends on whether the journalist contributes unique interpretation/analysis and the degree of employer control over the work product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers — bona fide professional teachers exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees whose primary duty is teaching, tutoring, instructing, or lecturing in the activity of imparting knowledge and who are employed as teachers by an educational establishment qualify as bona fide professional employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exempt teachers include regular academic teachers, kindergarten/nursery teachers, teachers of gifted/disabled children, vocational instructors, flight instructors, home economics, and music instructors. Possession of a teacher's certificate is clear evidence but not always required (e.g., higher education). The salary-level requirements of §541.300 and Subpart G do not apply to these teaching professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice of law or medicine — licensed practitioners and trainees
rubrics_metrics.description: Any employee holding a valid license or certificate permitting practice of law or medicine and actually engaged in practice qualifies as a bona fide professional; employees with the requisite medical academic degree engaged in internships/residencies also qualify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In medicine, the term 'physicians' includes MDs, DOs, podiatrists, dentists, optometrists, etc. The salary requirements of §541.300 and Subpart G do not apply to these employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer employees — general rule and duties test
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer systems analysts, computer programmers, software engineers and similar skilled computer workers are eligible for professional exemption if compensated at not less than §541.600 (or at least $27.63/hr under section 13(a)(17) for hourly) and their primary duty consists of: (1) applying systems analysis techniques (including consulting with users); (2) designing/developing/documenting/analyzing/creating/testing/modifying computer systems or programs based on user/system specifications; (3) designing/documenting/testing/creating/modifying programs related to machine operating systems; or (4) a combination requiring the same level of skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Job titles are not determinative of exemption applicability; the primary duty and skill level are controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer manufacture and repair exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer-occupation exemptions do not include employees engaged in the manufacture or repair of computer hardware and related equipment; employees whose work is highly dependent on computers but who are not primarily engaged in systems analysis/programming are also not exempt computer professionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: engineers, drafters using CAD are not exempt under the computer-employee professional exemption if their primary duties are not the enumerated computer professional tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer employees may meet executive/administrative exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer employees can qualify for executive or administrative exemptions if their primary duties include planning, scheduling, coordinating activities to develop systems to solve complex problems, or if a senior/lead programmer manages two or more other programmers in a recognized department and has hiring/firing/recommendation authority given particular weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination depends on whether the computer employee's duties align more closely with executive/administrative functions as described in Subparts B or C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside sales exemption — primary duty and regular away-from-business requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An outside salesperson is exempt if the primary duty is making sales (as defined in section 3(k)) or obtaining orders/contracts for services/use of facilities, and the employee is customarily and regularly engaged away from the employer's place(s) of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work incidental to the employee's own outside sales (deliveries, collections, sales reports, planning itineraries, attending sales conferences) is regarded as exempt outside sales work. The salary-level Subpart G does not apply to outside sales employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making sales — scope under section 3(k)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sales include transfer of title to tangible property and, in certain cases, tangible or valuable evidences of intangible property; 'sale' or 'sell' includes sale, exchange, contract to sell, consignment for sale, shipment for sale, or other disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exempt outside sales work includes sales of commodities and obtaining orders for services or use of facilities (e.g., selling radio/TV time, soliciting advertising, soliciting freight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Away from employer's place of business — definition and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside sales employees must be customarily and regularly engaged away from the employer's place(s) of business. Fixed sites used as a salesperson's headquarters or for telephonic solicitation are considered employer places of business. Sales by mail/telephone/Internet are not outside sales unless adjunct to personal calls. Displaying samples in hotel sample rooms during trips or at trade shows is not considered the employer's place of business if selling occurs (trade shows of short duration not considered the employer's place of business).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a location is an employer's place of business depends on use as a fixed site/headquarters; limited-duration sample rooms and trade shows are treated differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion work — exemption depends on relation to employee's own sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional work incidental to and in conjunction with an employee's own outside sales or solicitations is exempt; promotional work incidental to sales made by someone else is not exempt outside sales work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: manufacturer's rep performing promo activities that consummate their own sales can be exempt; company reps who arrange merchandise but do not obtain commitments for purchases are not exempt unless activities are in furtherance of the rep's own sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drivers who sell — primary-duty and factors for determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Drivers who deliver products and also sell may qualify as exempt outside sales employees only if the driver's primary duty is making sales. Incidental activities like loading/driving/delivering in conjunction with the driver's own sales are considered exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider: comparison of duties with other truck drivers/salespersons; possession of selling/solicitor license; customary/contractual arrangements about quantities to be delivered; collective-bargaining job descriptions; sales training; method of payment; proportion of earnings directly from sales. Examples of qualifying and nonqualifying drivers are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of drivers qualifying or not qualifying as outside sales employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualifying examples: (1) driver who is sole sales contact, takes orders, delivers from stock and is compensated commensurate with sales volume; (2) driver who obtains orders from persons with authority to commit purchases; (3) driver who calls on new prospects to obtain regular deliveries; (4) driver who persuades established customers to accept increased amounts/new products. Nonqualifying examples: route driver restocking vending machines, driver whose deliveries are routine and sales not affected by solicitation, driver primarily delivering and merchandising for others' sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether driving duties are primarily delivery or sales determines exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary requirements — standard salary level and territory variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard salary level to qualify as exempt executive/administrative/professional under section 13(a)(1) (exclusive of board/lodging): (1) beginning July 1, 2024: $844 per week; (2) beginning January 1, 2025: $1,128 per week; (3) as of July 1, 2027: level calculated pursuant to §541.607(b)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special lower salary levels apply to certain U.S. territories: CNMI/Guam/Puerto Rico/U.S. Virgin Islands: $455/week (non-Federal employers); American Samoa: $380/week (non-Federal employers). Administrative and professional employees may also be paid on a fee basis as defined in §541.605.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary requirement — frequency-of-payment equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: The weekly salary level requirement may be translated into equivalent amounts for pay periods longer than one week (e.g., $1,128/week equals $2,256 biweekly, $2,444 semimonthly, or $4,888 monthly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may convert the weekly threshold to the appropriate pay-frequency equivalent to determine compliance.
